content: Since the first recorded medical telephone consultation in 1879, the ability to conduct consultations over the phone has become a fundamental component of modern, patient-centered healthcare systems. Today, up to 25% of all care consultations are conducted via telephone. Research has demonstrated the impact of telephone consultations on clinicians' workloads and highlighted the need for quality improvement in this area. While clinicians typically receive training in communication and consultation skills, this training often does not address the unique challenges and requirements of telephone-based communication. Although some studies have evaluated the short-term effects of interventions designed to improve clinicians' telephone consultation skills, there is currently no systematic review that examines patient-centered outcomes or outcomes relevant to clinicians. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of training interventions aimed at improving clinicians' telephone consultation skills and their impact on patient outcomes. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and five other electronic databases, as well as two trial registries, up to May 19, 2016. Additional studies and data were identified through hand-searching references, checking citations, and contacting study authors. The review included randomized controlled trials, non-randomized controlled trials, controlled before-and-after studies, and interrupted time series studies that evaluated training interventions for improving clinicians' telephone consultation skills. These interventions were compared to any control intervention, including no intervention, and their impact on patient outcomes was assessed. Two independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias using Cochrane and EPOC guidelines. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. Study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary, and standard Cochrane methodological procedures were followed for data analysis. The review identified only one small controlled before-and-after study conducted in 1989. This study evaluated the effects of a training intervention on pediatric residents' history-taking and case management skills using a validated tool. The study found no difference in outcomes compared to no intervention. However, the authors did not report any quantitative analyses and were unable to provide additional data. The study was assessed as having a high risk of bias, and the certainty of the evidence was rated as very low using the GRADE framework. As a result, it remains uncertain whether this intervention improves clinicians' telephone consultation skills. Furthermore, no studies were identified that assessed the impact of training interventions on patient-centered primary outcomes, such as health outcomes measured by validated tools or biomedical markers, patient behaviors, morbidity or mortality, patient satisfaction, accuracy of urgency assessments, or adverse events. In conclusion, telephone consultation skills are part of a broader set of remote communication skills that are becoming increasingly important as healthcare delivery shifts toward remote and technology-supported models. However, there is currently no evidence specifically derived from studies on telephone consultations. As a result, the training of clinicians in this area must rely on studies and models based on face-to-face communication, which do not account for the distinct differences between these two modes of interaction. There is an urgent need for further research to evaluate the effects of various training interventions on clinicians' telephone consultation skills and their impact on patient outcomes.
